description: We are a group of Elmhurst University students.
summary:
ASTRA (Autonomous Space Telehealth & Risk Assessment) is an all-in-one health booth, and the software that runs it, for astronauts on long missions. Today the crew has to notice slow changes in their own health, such as poor sleep, fluid shifts, weight loss or low mood, and then wait for flight surgeons on Earth to review their data. On the way to Mars, each message can take up to 22 minutes.

ASTRA replaces a separate device for each measurement with one hands-free booth. The astronaut steps in, is recognised by face, and gets a facial scan. The booth then measures vitals, temperature, breathing and body mass, syncs their wristband, and adds experimental e-nose and blood-test readings. Next comes a short spoken interview whose follow-up questions depend on what the sensors found.

ASTRA compares every result with that astronaut’s own history, explains the findings in plain language on board, and queues a short, ranked report for Mission Control that tolerates delays. Everything runs offline, so the booth keeps working when Earth can’t respond. That makes the crew more independent, keeps flight surgeons’ attention on what matters, and suits remote settings on Earth such as Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics.
details:
What it does

ASTRA is a hands-free health booth and the software that runs it. Each day an astronaut steps in and completes a check-in of about five minutes without touching a screen:

  1. Identify. The booth recognizes the astronaut by face, with a liveness check so a photo can’t stand in for a person.
    • a vitals module: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen
    • a thermal camera: body temperature, breathing rate
    • a body-mass platform
    • a wristband that syncs sleep, resting heart rate, heart-rate variability and exercise
    • an experimental e-nose that tracks skin chemistry
    • a weekly blood-test panel
  2. Questions. A short spoken interview: how the astronaut is feeling, ratings from 1 to 10, and follow-up questions that depend on what the sensors found. For example, it asks about sleep only when sleep was short.
  3. Summary. ASTRA compares every reading and answer with that astronaut’s own history and explains the results aloud in plain language. Each result gets a clear status: normal, watch, concern or urgent.
  4. Mission Control. Anything worth a flight surgeon’s attention goes into a delay-tolerant, store-and-forward queue. Mission Control receives a short, ranked report instead of raw data.

An emergency mode is always one step away. All of this runs fully offline.

How it works

  • Personal baselines, not population norms. For each astronaut we compute a robust baseline: the median and the median absolute deviation, plus a Theil–Sen trend to catch slow drift. An IsolationForest model flags unusual combinations of readings, so a value that is “normal” for most people can still be flagged as unusual for this person.
  • Offline speech. faster-whisper handles speech-to-text on the CPU, and Kokoro handles text-to-speech, with Piper as a fallback. Replies are spoken sentence by sentence, so the voice starts within about half a second.
  • Recognition. Face recognition uses OpenCV’s YuNet and SFace models, accepting a match only after three consecutive frames and a micro-motion liveness check. MediaPipe FaceLandmarker supplies the facial geometry.
  • Prototype honesty. In this prototype the medical sensors are simulated, using deterministic, physiologically plausible data. The camera, microphone, speech and analysis are real.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and SQLite, and Pydantic
  • Machine learning and vision: OpenCV (YuNet, SFace), MediaPipe, scikit-learn, faster-whisper, and Kokoro and Piper TTS
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Three Fiber (an interactive 3D booth), Framer Motion and Recharts
  • Development: Git, plus AI-assisted coding and design tools
  • Hardware for the demo: a standard laptop with a webcam and microphone. No cloud services or internet connection are needed.

Benefits and intended impact

  • For astronauts: the crew no longer has to spot slow changes in themselves, because the booth checks every day and answers on board in minutes instead of waiting on Earth.
  • For the mission: one booth replaces a string of separate devices. Flight surgeons get a ranked summary that survives communication delays and blackouts.
  • On Earth: the same offline booth fits places where help is far away, such as Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics.

What makes it creative

To our knowledge, no existing system combines all-in-one sensing, an adaptive spoken interview and on-board assessment against each person’s own history. The booth’s questions are driven by its sensor readings, so every check-in is different.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay and blackouts: everything runs offline and reports are queued, so Earth is never in the critical path.
  • Busy crews: the check-in is hands-free, takes about five minutes, can be done entirely by voice, and has a manual fallback.
  • Privacy and safety: all data stays on board in a local database, and identity is checked for liveness.
  • Trust: results use plain language and consistent status colors, and every flag shows which reading triggered it and how it compares with the astronaut’s own usual values.
  • Limitations: the medical sensors are simulated for now, and the e-nose and on-board blood analysis are still research areas.

What’s next

  • Replace the simulated sensors with real devices.
  • Fine-tune a model on medical data for a more accurate assessment.
  • Explore retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and LLM assistance.
  • Research on-board blood analysis and e-nose technology further.
  • Pitch the idea to potential investors.
